tarpon: Tarpon. The silver king. Scales as big as your palm and a mouth like a bucket. Hook one, and the whole fish leaves the water.
snook: Snook. See that one black stripe down the side, like somebody drew it with a marker? Nothing else wears it. My nephew Matt caught a monster at South Point.
trout: Seatrout. Looks like somebody shook a pepper shaker over him. Soft mouth, so you never yank. Grass beds mean trout.
intro: I’m Dan. Around here, folks just call me Uncle Dan. You can’t guide a boat full of people if you can’t tell them what just swam past, flew over or slid off the bank. So we’re going to learn Florida’s animals the way I learned them: look for the one thing that gives each of them away. Start with a dozen. I’ll be right here.
redfish: Redfish. Copper colored, with a black spot by the tail like a thumbprint. Some folks call him spot-tail. It was the first keeper Matt ever caught.
snapper: Mangrove snapper. Gray-bronze, with a dark stripe through the eye like a bandit’s mask. They call him snapper for a reason. Mind your fingers.
sheepshead: Sheepshead. Striped like an old-time convict, with a mouthful of teeth that look like yours. Best bait thief on any dock.
black-drum: Black drum. The redfish’s gray cousin. No spot on the tail, and whiskers under his chin for feeling out crabs in the mud.
flounder: Flounder. Flat as a dinner plate, with both eyes on one side of his head. He lies on the bottom looking like sand, and waits.
ladyfish: Ladyfish. Skinny, silver, and she spends the whole fight jumping. Fun to catch. Slippery as soap to hold.
jack: Jack crevalle. Bulldog forehead, yellowish tail, black spot on the gill. Pound for pound he pulls harder than anything in the bay.
mullet: Mullet. Blunt nose, silver, and he jumps for no reason anybody’s ever proven. You won’t hook him, but everything you want eats him.
catfish: Hardhead catfish. Whiskers and three sharp spines that sting. Don’t grab him. Use the pliers.
pinfish: Pinfish. Hand-sized, with a row of needles down his back. That’s bait, son. Hold him from underneath.
pufferfish: Pufferfish. Get him mad and he blows up like a prickly ball. Got a beak that’ll clip your hook, too. And never eat one. He’s poison.
bonefish: Bonefish. The gray ghost. Silver, with his mouth tucked underneath. He feeds in water so thin his tail sticks out.
cobia: Cobia. Long, brown, flat head. Half the people who see one yell shark. Look for the pale stripe down his side.
grouper: Grouper. Big head, bigger mouth, blotchy like camouflage. Hook him and he has one plan: get back under his rock.
yellowtail: Yellowtail snapper. Follow the yellow stripe from his nose and it runs right into a forked yellow tail. Reef fish. Good eating.
amberjack: Amberjack. Big bronze brute off the wrecks. See the dark stripe from his nose up through his eye? They call him the reef donkey, because he pulls like one.
lionfish: Lionfish. Zebra stripes and a fan of spines that’ll sting you good. Pretty, and he doesn’t belong here. He eats the reef’s baby fish.
brim: Bluegill. Round as a saucer, with a dark flap behind the gill. Folks call him brim. First fish most kids ever catch.
permit: Permit. Tall, flat and silver, with long dark fins like sickles. The pickiest fish on the flats. Guides brag about one for a year.
pompano: Pompano. Looks like a permit’s little brother. Yellow on the throat and belly, shorter fins. He runs the beach in the surf.
spanish-mackerel: Spanish mackerel. Slim, silver, with gold spots down his side. Teeth like razors. Bring pliers.
tripletail: Tripletail. Count the tails: looks like three. He floats on his side by a crab trap buoy, pretending to be a leaf.
king-mackerel: King mackerel. Kingfish. Bigger than the Spanish and no gold spots. Look at the line on his side: it takes a sharp dip.
barracuda: Barracuda. A silver torpedo with an underbite full of fangs. He’ll follow the boat just to look at you. Don’t dangle anything shiny.
goliath-grouper: Goliath grouper. Big as a refrigerator, with little bitty eyes and a round tail. He’ll eat the fish right off your line and never say thank you.
red-snapper: Red snapper. Rosy red from nose to tail, even his eye. He lives deep, way offshore, and everybody wants him for supper.
hogfish: Hogfish. Long snout like a pig, for rooting in the sand, and three long streamers on his back. Prettiest thing on the reef.
mahi: Mahi-mahi. Some call him dolphin, but he’s no relation to Flipper. Green and gold like a neon sign, and a forehead like a brick.
sailfish: Sailfish. A spear on his nose and a blue sail on his back that he raises like a flag. Florida’s own saltwater fish. Fast as a pickup truck.
wahoo: Wahoo. Tiger stripes down his sides and a snout like a beak. When he takes the bait, the reel screams, and so does everybody on the boat.
triggerfish: Triggerfish. Flat, gray and tough as a boot. The spine on his back locks straight up, and only he knows where the trigger is.
blackfin-tuna: Blackfin tuna. Built like a football that somebody taught to swim. Dark back, a bronze stripe on his side, and he never stops moving.
largemouth-bass: Largemouth bass. Green, with a dark jagged stripe down the side. Close his mouth and the jaw reaches back past his eye. King of every Florida lake.
crappie: Black crappie. Speckled perch, we call him. Silver with black freckles all over, and a mouth as thin as paper. Go easy.
peacock-bass: Peacock bass. Gold, with three dark bars and a spot on his tail like the eye on a peacock feather. He lives in the canals down around Miami.
gar: Gar. Looks like a log with a long toothy snout. His scales are hard as armor. He’s been swimming these waters since the dinosaurs.
bull-shark: Bull shark. Thick, plain gray, with a short blunt nose. He’s the one that swims right up the rivers into fresh water. Give him room.
bowfin: Bowfin. Mudfish. One long fin runs down most of his back, and there’s a dark spot by his tail. He can gulp air, so mud doesn’t bother him.
blacktip-shark: Blacktip. Slim, pointed nose, and it looks like he dipped his fins in ink. He’ll jump clear out of the water and spin like a top.
lemon-shark: Lemon shark. Yellowish, like the name says. Here’s the trick: look at the two fins on his back. They’re nearly the same size.
nurse-shark: Nurse shark. Brown, sleepy, lying on the bottom with two little whiskers by his mouth. Laziest shark in Florida. Leave him be, and don’t pull his tail.
tiger-shark: Tiger shark. Dark bars down his sides when he’s young, and a nose as wide and square as a shovel. He’ll eat anything. They’ve found license plates in there.
hammerhead-shark: Hammerhead. You won’t mix this one up. Head like a hammer, eyes way out on the ends, and a back fin tall as a sail.
bonnethead: Bonnethead. The hammerhead’s little cousin. Maybe a yard long, with a head rounded like a shovel. He eats crabs on the flats.
mako-shark: Mako. Blue as the deep water he lives in, with a pointed nose and teeth that show even when his mouth is shut. Fastest shark there is.
whale-shark: Whale shark. Biggest fish in the whole ocean, covered in white spots like a checkerboard. And all he eats is tiny stuff. Gentle as a cow.
great-white: Great white. Heavy as a truck, gray on top and white below, with a sharp line between. He comes south in the winter, way offshore, like a snowbird.
stingray: Stingray. A flat brown diamond with a whip for a tail and a barb on it. He hides in the sand, so shuffle your feet when you wade.
alligator: Alligator. Dark, nearly black, with a wide round snout like the letter U. Fresh water is his home. Never, ever feed one.
sawfish: Sawfish. A snout like a hedge trimmer, teeth down both sides. There aren’t many left, and the Everglades is their nursery. See one, and you’ve seen something.
manta-ray: Manta ray. Wings as wide as a boat, black on top, white below, with two flaps by his mouth like horns. No stinger. He just flies along, eating soup.
water-snake: Banded water snake. Slimmer than a moccasin, narrow head, round eyes. Not venomous. But you don’t need to sort them out up close. Leave every snake alone, and you’ll never be wrong.
cottonmouth: Cottonmouth. Water moccasin. Thick, dark, with a head like a brick. When he’s had enough of you he opens his mouth, and it’s white as cotton. He’s venomous, and that’s your invitation to leave.
crocodile: Crocodile. Lighter colored, with a narrow pointed snout like the letter V, and teeth showing top and bottom. He likes salty water, down at the south tip of Florida, where you can find gators and crocs both. Give him room.
coral-snake: Coral snake. Red, yellow and black rings, and a black nose. Here’s the rhyme my daddy taught me: red touches yellow, dangerous fellow. Look, and walk away.
scarlet-kingsnake: Scarlet kingsnake. He wears the coral snake’s colors, but in a different order, and his nose is red. Red touches black, friend of Jack. Not venomous. Still, hands off.
diamondback: Eastern diamondback. Biggest rattlesnake there is. Dark diamonds down his back, and a rattle on the end. When you hear that buzz, freeze, then back away slow. Don’t go looking for him.
corn-snake: Corn snake. Orange with red blotches outlined in black. Some call him the red rat snake, because that’s what he eats. A good neighbor to have around a barn.
pygmy-rattlesnake: Pygmy rattler. Not much longer than your forearm. Gray with dark blotches and a rusty stripe down the back. His rattle’s so small it sounds like a bug. He’s venomous, so watch where you put your hands.
black-racer: Black racer. Skinny, plain black, white chin, and fast. By the time you say there’s a snake, he’s in the next county. Not venomous. Let him go.
indigo-snake: Indigo snake. Long as a canoe paddle and thick as your wrist, shiny blue-black like a new truck. Gentle, and getting rare. If you see one, count yourself lucky.
iguana: Green iguana. Long as a canoe paddle, tail and all, with spines down his back and a flap under his chin. He’s not from here either. On a cold morning they fall right out of the trees.
python: Burmese python. Tan with brown blotches like a giraffe, and as big around as a grown man’s leg. He doesn’t belong in the Everglades. Somebody’s pet got loose, and now there are thousands.
anole: Green anole. Little green lizard, long as your finger, on every porch rail in Florida. Watch him puff out that pink throat to show off.
gopher-tortoise: Gopher tortoise. He lives on land, not in the water. High domed shell and front legs like shovels. He digs a burrow that a hundred other critters move into.
loggerhead: Loggerhead. Sea turtle with a head like a block of wood, built for crunching crabs. The mamas crawl up Florida’s beaches on summer nights to lay their eggs.
green-turtle: Green sea turtle. Small round head and a smooth shell with streaks like a sunburst. He grazes on seagrass like a cow in a pasture.
softshell-turtle: Softshell turtle. Flat as a pancake, with a leathery shell and a nose like a snorkel. Long neck, too, and he can reach around and bite. Hands off the pancake.
pelican: Brown pelican. Big pouch under the bill, and he dives headfirst like he fell off a roof. We’ve got two regulars out back of my place, Bertha and Oscar.
white-pelican: White pelican. A good bit bigger than the brown one, bright white, orange bill. He doesn’t dive. He paddles along with his friends and scoops. Comes down for the winter, like half of Ohio.
great-blue-heron: Great blue heron. Tall as a fourth-grader, blue-gray, with a bill like a dagger. He stands still as a fence post. If he’s standing where you’re headed, it’s too shallow.
great-egret: Great egret. Tall, all white, yellow bill, black legs. An egret is a white heron, more or less. Remember him by the yellow bill.
snowy-egret: Snowy egret. Smaller than the great egret, with a black bill and black legs, and then bright yellow feet. Looks like he’s wearing golden slippers.
ibis: White ibis. White bird with a long red bill curved down like a hook, for poking in the mud. They walk across lawns in a line, like they’re looking for a lost contact lens.
wood-stork: Wood stork. Big white bird with a bald, wrinkly gray head. Not a handsome fellow. Old-timers call him flinthead. He fishes by feel, with his bill open in the water.
spoonbill: Roseate spoonbill. Pink bird, and half the tourists yell flamingo. Look at the bill. It’s flat and round on the end like a wooden spoon, and he swings it side to side.
flamingo: Flamingo. The real thing: taller, pinker, with a neck like a garden hose and a bill bent in the middle with a black tip. They’re rare in the wild here, so when you see one, tell everybody.
osprey: Osprey. The fish hawk. White head with a dark mask through the eye, white belly. He hovers, folds up, and hits the water feet first. Best fisherman in Florida, and he knows it.
bald-eagle: Bald eagle. Dark brown body, white head, white tail, big yellow beak. Bigger than the osprey, and not above stealing the osprey’s fish right out of the air.
hawk: Red-shouldered hawk. Rusty chest, black-and-white striped tail, and the loudest voice in the swamp. He sits on a wire and screams his own name. Kee-yer, kee-yer.
falcon: Peregrine falcon. Pointed wings, gray back, and a dark helmet with a mustache. When he dives on a bird, he’s the fastest animal on earth. Faster than a race car.
anhinga: Anhinga. Snakebird. He swims with just that long neck sticking out, and spears fish on a bill straight as a needle. Then he hangs his wings out to dry like laundry.
cormorant: Cormorant. Looks like an anhinga until you check the bill. His is hooked on the end, and he’s got an orange patch on the throat. They line up on channel markers like they’re waiting for a bus.
frigatebird: Frigatebird. Man-o’-war bird. Long skinny wings bent like a boomerang, and a tail forked like scissors. He can stay up for days, and he almost never lands on the water. Fishermen follow him to find fish.
skimmer: Black skimmer. Look at that bill: red and black, and the bottom half is longer than the top. He flies along with it slicing the water, and snaps shut on whatever he bumps.
sandhill-crane: Sandhill crane. Tall, gray, with a red cap on his forehead. You’ll see a pair strolling a golf course like they own it. And that rattling bugle call carries a mile.
vulture: Turkey vulture. Buzzard, we say. Little bald red head, and he holds his wings up in a V and wobbles like he’s had too much coffee. He’s the cleanup crew. Be grateful.
gull: Laughing gull. Gray wings, white belly, and in summer a black hood. Sounds exactly like he’s laughing at your casting. Guard your sandwich.
owl: Barred owl. Round head, no ears showing, big dark eyes. You’ll hear him before you see him. He’s the one asking: who cooks for you? Who cooks for you-all?
kingfisher: Kingfisher. Blue-gray, with a shaggy crest like he just woke up, and a bill too big for his body. He hovers over the creek, then dives. Makes a rattle like a broken reel.
manatee: Manatee. Sea cow. Big, gray, slow and gentle, with a tail like a paddle. Mostly you’ll see a nose come up to breathe. Slow the boat right down. Look, don’t touch.
dolphin: Bottlenose dolphin. See a fin and can’t tell? Watch the tail. A dolphin’s tail beats up and down, so his back rolls over the top. A shark’s tail sweeps side to side.
panther: Florida panther. Big tan cat, no spots, with a long, heavy rope of a tail. There are only a couple hundred left in the whole world, and they all live here. Most Floridians never see one.
black-bear: Black bear. The only bear we’ve got. Black coat, tan muzzle. He’d rather have your garbage than have anything to do with you. Give him the whole road.
bobcat: Bobcat. Twice the size of a house cat, spotted, with a stub of a tail. That’s the tell: short tail, bobcat. Long tail, panther.
otter: River otter. Long, sleek and brown, with whiskers and a thick tail. He’ll pop up by the boat, give you a look, and go right back to playing. Happiest animal in the swamp.
raccoon: Raccoon. Black mask, ringed tail, and hands like a burglar. He’ll open your cooler, eat your bait, and wash his hands after. Latch everything.
key-deer: Key deer. A whole deer about the size of a big dog. They live down in the Keys and no place else on earth. They get tame and will walk right up to you. Don’t feed them, and don’t walk up to them.
stone-crab: Stone crab. Heavy brown shell, and big claws with black tips that can crack an oyster. Best eating in Florida. Keep your fingers out of there.
armadillo: Armadillo. A possum in a suit of armor. Nine bands across his middle and a long nose for digging up bugs. Scare him, and he jumps straight up in the air.
blue-crab: Blue crab. Blue claws, a sharp point on each side of the shell, and back legs shaped like paddles. He swims sideways, fast, and he pinches like he means it.
horseshoe-crab: Horseshoe crab. A brown helmet with a spike for a tail. Looks scary. Completely harmless. His family has been walking these beaches since before the dinosaurs.
lobster: Spiny lobster. Florida’s lobster has no big claws at all. Just two long whips for antennae and spines all over. He walks the reef at night, backwards when he’s scared.
thresher: Thresher shark. Look at that tail. It’s as long as the rest of him. He cracks it like a whip to knock fish silly, then circles back to eat them.
sharpnose: Sharpnose shark. A little fellow, maybe a yard long, with a long pointed nose and white freckles on his sides. Most of the small sharks you’ll catch off the beach are him.
spinner-shark: Spinner shark. The blacktip’s twin, nearly. Longer nose, and a black tip on every single fin. He comes up through a school of bait spinning like a drill and jumps clear out of the water.
sandbar-shark: Sandbar shark. See how tall that back fin is? Like a sail, and set way up front over his shoulders. That’s the fin they put in the movies.
eagle-ray: Spotted eagle ray. Dark back covered in white spots and rings, and a snout like a duck’s bill. He flies through the water like a bird, and now and then he jumps clean out of it.
reef-shark: Caribbean reef shark. He’s the gray shark the divers see cruising the coral down in the Keys. No stripes, no spots, just a dusky edge on his fins and tail. He owns that reef, and he knows it.
rat-snake: Yellow rat snake. Long, yellow, with four dark stripes from his neck to his tail. Chicken snake, we call him. Best climber in the woods. He’ll go straight up a tree trunk. Not venomous.
green-snake: Rough green snake. Thin as a pencil and green as a new leaf. He lives up in the bushes and vines, eating crickets, and you’ll walk past ten for every one you see. Gentle as they come. Not venomous.
garter-snake: Garter snake. Three pale stripes down a dark body, one on top and one down each side. In Florida the stripes often run a little blue. The first snake most kids ever meet. Not venomous. Let him go on his way.
ringneck: Ringneck snake. No bigger than a pencil, dark gray, with a bright ring around his neck like a collar. Scare him and he curls up his tail to show you an orange belly. You’ll find him under a flowerpot.
copperhead: Copperhead. Tan, with dark bands pinched in the middle like an hourglass, and a head the color of a new penny. In Florida you’ll only find him up in the Panhandle. He’s venomous, and he hides in dead leaves, so watch your feet.
hognose: Hognose snake. Turned-up nose like a pig. Now here’s the best actor in Florida. Bother him and he flattens his neck like a cobra and hisses. If that doesn’t work, he rolls over and plays dead with his tongue hanging out. It’s all an act. Leave him to it.
timber-rattlesnake: Timber rattlesnake. Canebrake, the old folks say. Black bands shaped like a V, a rusty stripe down his backbone, and a black velvet tail with a rattle on it. North Florida woods and river swamps. Venomous. Back away slow.
